newsitem.title: GERMANY: Come to America, SEC tells German firms.
newsitem.headline: Come to America, SEC tells German firms.

text.p: German companies should drop their qualms about stringent U.S. accounting rules and take up the challenge of listing their shares in the U.S., New York's Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) says.
"There is no better time than now to access the U.S. capital markets," SEC chairman Arthur Levitt told a reception for German corporations in Frankfurt late on Thursday.
"We want your companies on our shores."

Levitt, in Germany for a day as part of a tour to promote U.S. capital markets, said he expected announcements about plans for New York listings from several large German firms in the coming weeks, but declined to be more specific.

To date, the only German blue chips with full New York listings are Daimler-Benz AG and newly floated telecoms giant Deutsche Telekom. Chemicals firm Hoechst AG and utility group Veba AG are expected to follow suit soon.
The main stumbling block for German firms considering accessing U.S. capital markets is U.S. accounting rules, which demand significantly more transparency than the German norm.
Despite an increased emphasis on shareholder value here, a switch to U.S. accounting is still widely perceived as too expensive and unrealistic.
But Levitt said the rewards of a U.S. listing, in terms of increased profile and better managerial control on the back of greater transparency, outweighed the costs of a new accounting procedure.

German firms had nothing to fear from the perceived bureaucracy of the SEC, Levitt said, pledging that the commission would offer help such as legal advice and general confidential consultation to companies interested in the U.S.
"The Commission wants companies to access U.S. markets and will do all it can to encourage it," Levitt said.
He also said the SEC was open to accepting listings from foreign companies adopting International Accounting Standards (IAS), provided that an acceptable standard for these rules is reached.
The only acceptable formula for the SEC would be a comprehensive and high quality generally accepted basis of accounting, which is "rigorously interpreted and applied", Levitt said.
A lot of work needed to be done before an acceptable proposal could be submitted, Levitt said.
"The SEC will not compromise the safeguards already existing for U.S. investors," he said.
